items.title: Show HN: aiport – A self-improving local LLM gateway for the erratic vibe coder
items.story_key: story|variant:coder|title:aiport a self improving local llm gateway for the erratic vibe coder
items.content_excerpt: If you're an erratic vibe coder, you know the day: Claude Code in one repo, Codex in another, a model on Ollama or llama.cpp, and credits on Bedrock, Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta. You switch models by task, sometimes mid-task, and jump between projects several times an hour. The apps you build call those models too, so each one ends up re-wiring the same providers. You can't see which app called what, and you find out about failures when something breaks. aiport is a Go program that runs on your machine (loopback only) and sits between your apps, your coding agents and the providers. aiport watches how your apps use models and proposes changes. Nothing is applied without your approval unless you turn that on, and every change can be reverted. Applications call aiport with their own token. aiport routes each call to the provider you chose, keeps the metadata, and turns repeated failures into Issues you can fix from the dashboard, or hand to the application's coding agent. You need Go 1.27+ ( brew install go , or go.dev/dl ). Dependencies are vendored and the dashboard is pre-built, so nothing else is downloaded. Or install the binary without cloning: go install github.com/harelix/aiport/cmd/aiport@latest (it lands in $(go env GOPATH)/bin ; run aiport init and aiport serve ). Open the dashboard address serve prints ( http://127.0.0.1:8787/ by default; init --listen picks another, and you can use aiport.localhost instead ), paste the management token and set a password. Paste your provider keys on Providers , then Check connection on each card: it makes one free GET /models call and generates nothing. Start any local provider (Ollama, llama.cpp) yourself. The manual covers every page. It is also built into the dashboard: press the help button, or the ⓘ next to any section. init writes aiport.yaml and a private aiport.yaml.env (mode 0600) for local tokens and the keys you paste in the dashboard. It never overwrites a file, and provider keys never go into YAML. Provider presets: openai , anthropic , bedrock , meta , ollama , llamacpp . See the configuration reference and aiport.example.yaml . aiport is experimental. No provider and coding-agent combination has passed the live compatibility gate yet. Token counts and cost are not measured. A provider must speak the protocol of the client calling it, since aiport does not translate. items.title: Show HN: RepoMagpie – your coding agent remembers the repos you've tried
items.summary: While building projects, I kept searching the internet for resources, repos and skill sets. One day I noticed something: why isn’t there a single repo that collects all of these in one place and makes them usable? That’s why I built this.
items.story_key: story|title:repomagpie your coding agent remembers the repos you ve tried
items.content_excerpt: RepoMagpie: your coding agent remembers the repos you’ve tried, and what you thought of them. RepoMagpie is your personal journal of the open-source repos and tools you've tried (libraries, CLIs, MCP servers, agent skills), with your own verdict on each. Your coding agent checks it before it picks a tool: it suggests what worked for you, and it stops on what you ruled out. Months ago you tried pdfkit and gave up on it. Today your agent is about to install it again, and in Claude Code, RepoMagpie's hook asks you first, with your own note: It works in seven coding agents , among them Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor and Gemini CLI. Everything stays local: plain Markdown files on your machine, no account, no cloud server. For teams, the same notes can live in the repository and be shared through git ( below ). Status: stable and in active development. The changelog lists every version; the roadmap shows what comes next. setup shows which files it will change, asks first, and backs up each file it edits; repomagpie setup --dry-run only shows the plan ( agents ). doctor also lists setup 's backups, which can hold your agents' secrets ( SECURITY.md ); repomagpie setup --delete-backups deletes them. Write your first note. A GitHub URL also fetches the repository's licence, topics and agent skills, and --use-when lets you find the note later by what you need: GitHub allows 60 requests an hour without a token. To raise the limit, sign in with the GitHub CLI ( gh auth login ): RepoMagpie uses its login. Or set GITHUB_TOKEN or GH_TOKEN . repomagpie doctor says which one it uses. RepoMagpie comes only from this repository , the npm package repomagpie and the agent skill on skills.sh . There are no installers, no .exe or other downloads, no other packages and no other website: anything else that calls itself RepoMagpie is not ours ( SECURITY.md ). Before your agent picks a tool, the skill tells it to check your journals: search or suggest while it chooses, and recall before an install, as MCP tools or repomagpie commands. Your verdicts come back first. What worked for you is suggested; when a note says to avoid a package, your agent shows it to you and asks first. The hook checks the install command itself, in case the agent skips that step. There is no extra model, no API key and no telemetry. RepoMagpie works as well as your agent follows the skill; without a hook, that includes the check before an install. What repomagpie setup sets up in each agent, on Linux, Windows

items.title: Four Bugs, One Day: What a Self-Policing Agent Org Looks Like When It Works
items.story_key: story|title:four bugs one day what a self policing agent org looks like when it works
items.content_excerpt: Most engineering blog posts describe a system the authors built. This one describes a system that caught its own bugs. On 2026-06-10, the autonomous agent organization that runs agent.ceo found, root-caused, fixed, and verified four distinct platform bugs in a single working day — not because someone scheduled a bug hunt, but because the agents hit the bugs in the course of their ordinary work and refused to let them slide. We think that's the more interesting story: not "agents can write code," but "an agent organization can police itself." 1. A task that lost its acceptance. Our task system assigns work over a real-time message bus and also writes a durable record of every task. The bug: the assignment was published before the durable record was created . Fast auto-accepts — arriving about a second later — looked up a record that didn't exist yet and were silently dropped. Then the late-arriving create overwrote the status back to "assigned." The symptom was a stream of false "nobody accepted this" escalations and tasks whose timestamps lagged by 30–50 seconds. The fix was an ordering change — create the durable record before publishing the notification — plus a guard that refuses to clobber a newer status, plus a loud warning on the path that used to fail silently. Six regression tests now hold the line. 2. A test pretending to be real work. This one is our favorite, because of how it was caught. A set of test fixtures — fake tasks that exist only to exercise the code — leaked past their mocks and landed in the real task registry. The next time an agent asked "what should I work on?", it was handed a fabricated task marked URGENT , complete with plausible-sounding business context. The agent didn't run it. It noticed that nobody had assigned this work and flagged it instead of executing. That instinct — provenance-check unrecognized urgent work before acting on it — is the difference between an automated script and an accountable worker. The fix makes the failure structurally impossible: the test harness now redirects all registry paths to a throwaway temporary directory before any storage layer is even instantiated. Tests can no longer touch production stores, by construction. 3. An API that said "200" while doing nothing. A queue filter that skips test-prefixed items — sensible for creating throwaway resources — was also silently skipping the deletion of those resources, while the delete endpoint cheerfully returned 200 OK . items.title: RIVER: Evidence-guided multi-agent retrieval for enzyme--reaction discovery
items.summary: Enzyme function annotation and the identification of candidate enzymes for a given reaction are essential steps in connecting genomic information to biochemical reaction networks. However, existing methods rely on sequence or structural similarity or on training with known enzyme--reaction pairs, making it difficult to integrate biochemical evidence across large candidate spaces; they also struggle with retrieval tasks involving enzyme families whose members are highly similar. Here, we introduce RIVER (Reaction--enzyme Inference via Evidence-guided Retrieval), a multi-agent framework for bidirectional enzyme--reaction retrieval that identifies potentially catalyzed reactions for a given enzyme and ranks candidate enzymes for a given reaction. RIVER coordinates large language models, specialized biochemical computational tools, and external knowledge resources to assemble evidence at multiple levels, including reaction chemistry, protein sequences and domains, catalytic mechanisms, and database annotations. Dedicated validation modules further examine evidence gaps and potential conflicts and rerank candidates using traceable evidence records. On public benchmarks, RIVER achieves the highest success rates in both enzyme retrieval and enzyme annotation. In family-specific enzyme retrieval, RIVER outperforms the evaluated baselines on the selected datasets and metrics. In Escherichia coli enzyme retrieval tasks constructed from recent literature, RIVER achieves the best retrieval results with closed-source and open-source model configurations, substantially outperforming closed-source general-purpose and biology-specialized multi-agent systems, including Claude Code, Codex, and Phylo Max. These results suggest that evidence-guided multi-agent retrieval can prioritize biochemically supported enzyme--reaction relationships, providing a basis for subsequent experimental validation.

items.title: Scientist World: Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists
items.summary: AI-Scientists arrived, but a world for them to grow in did not. Human scientists take theirs for granted $-$ centuries of open problems and shared ideas, waiting in the scientific literature. To AI-Scientists, that world is readable but not runnable, so we build Scientist World for them: every research paper becomes an executable environment. Our autonomous pipeline extracts each paper's open-ended research question and reproduces its proposed method as the baseline; an AI-Scientist entering the environment is evaluated against what the human authors achieved. We release the first 1,000 verified environments. With the world as an evaluation, we found that frontier AI-Scientists can already surpass the human researchers 74% of the time. As a record of how AI does science, it contains 6,400 hours of research traces, with every idea, experiment, failure, and success. As a training ground, we are able to raise (+158%) a small model to match frontier models in research ideation. At last, AI-Scientists' own world has arrived, grown from and growing with science itself.

items.title: Introducing Kinference: An Open Source Inference Control Plane for vLLM and Kubernetes
items.summary: Kinference is a new open source inference control plane for building scalable inference platforms with vLLM and Kubernetes, providing token rate limiting, tenant usage and cost tracking, intelligent load balancing, and inference policies.
items.story_key: model:vllm|title:introducing kinference an open source inference control plane for vllm and kuber
items.content_excerpt: We’re excited to announce Kinference [kay-inference] , a new open source project for building scalable inference platforms with vLLM. We created Kinference at Buoyant after watching our customers struggle to run open weight models in their environments. We designed Kinference to be the control plane layer for the platform you need to build. It uses vLLM to do the underlying inference, and provides the set of features necessary for building an inference platform in practice. This includes token rate limiting, tenant usage and cost tracking, intelligent load balancing, and inference policies. Kinference can be paired with your existing stack. Using Kinference is simply a matter of pointing inference clients to its HTTP endpoint and sending OpenAI or Anthropic-compatible inference traffic there. Kinference serves a heterogeneous, evolving set of models running on a heterogeneous, evolving pool of GPUs, to a heterogenous, evolving set of clients.. In addition to policies and a routing layer, Kinference provides inference-specific load balancing that takes into account signals like GPU queue sizes, historical performance, and the contents of the KV cache on the GPU. This KV-cache awareness, in particular, allows Kinference to send requests to the vLLM worker that will do the least work for that specific request. Modeling the KV cache content of the GPU can produce dramatic gains in performance for distributed inference. For example, in our public Kinference benchmarks , we showed that, when compared to standard Kubernetes load balancing (labeled “service” below), Kinference (labeled “kinference”) was able to cut median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 95% and median end-to-end latency by 45% of requests on one workload type. By incorporating cache awareness into policies, platform owners can create policies that will send simple requests to the cheaper model — but only if that’s less work than sending them to the expensive model in the first place. In our unloaded latency benchmark above, we sought to measure the effect of Kinference’s KV-cache-aware load balancing in isolation. In our capacity benchmark, below, we measured the requests per minute can each endpoint can serve within a latency SLO. In the capacity benchmark, Kinference served 7.4× the goodput on shared-prefix and about 3.5× the goodput on multiturn . It was able to attain our chosen SLO at concurrency 32 (the highest measured) on our shared-prefix workload, and concurrency 8 on the multiturn workloa

items.title: Why human insight is a strategic advantage for building better agents
items.summary: Explore 3 principles for effective human-in-the-loop workflows and how human-review is a strategic imperative for production-ready agents.
items.story_key: story|title:why human insight is a strategic advantage for building better agents
items.content_excerpt: As agents take on longer, more complex tasks, evaluating their performance means looking beyond the final AI-generated answer. Human review plays an important role in agent development: it helps teams define what good looks like, evaluate performance in context, and turn expert judgment into data that drives improvement. In this blog, we explore three principles for effective human-in-the-loop workflows: defining quality through expert judgment, evaluating agents in context, and turning human feedback into reusable evaluation data that drives continuous improvement. An agent trace is a record of everything an agent did in a single attempt: user messages, model responses, tool calls, and intermediate steps. Teams use traces to debug behavior, score quality, and decide what to fix. Often an engineer or an online evaluator flags a trace when something looks off. The flag is a signal, not an explanation. It usually is not enough to know how to change the agent. The flagged trace goes into an annotation queue . A human reviewer opens the interaction and leaves feedback: did the agent do the right thing, and why or why not? Automation chooses what to review. The human supplies the judgment that builders act on. In LangSmith , a queue item can be one run (a single step or span) or a thread (the full multi-turn session). With a thread, the reviewer sees the conversation the user had, instead of one step cut out of it. Each reviewer brings domain judgment the trace does not contain on its own: what “good” means in that job, what the user was trying to do, and what the agent should have done instead. This expert judgment is often highly specific to the company, role, or individual's expertise, and is a key part of building differentiated agents. Or as Snoop Dogg put in his commencement speech at CSU Long Beach : “Nobody can do you, like you do.” When a domain expert reviews a trace, one of the most valuable parts of the review is their reason. An expert can say why an output was right or wrong, and how a high-quality agent should behave. While reviewers can catch what automated evals miss, they also surface problems that sit beside the agent’s answer. For example, they might discover that an eval is scoring the wrong behavior, or that there is a gap in the rubric. One note in a queue can reveal a broader pattern worth fixing in the evaluator itself. This expert feedback changes the evaluations, and ultimately how the agent is built. items.title: Maggie Appleton: Agentic Coding Has Outgrown the Text Box
items.summary:
Agentic coding has outgrown the text box. Maggie Appleton, staff research engineer at GitHub Next, argues that walls of CLI output and AGENTS.md files serve coding agents far better than the humans steering them. She walks through Chopin, the GitHub Next prototype where background agents turn a team's planning chat into a structured plan, and makes the case for agents that prompt you instead of waiting to be prompted.

What we cover:
– Why text-heavy agentic coding tools favor agents over humans
– Boundary objects: what AGENTS.md, skill files and MCP servers get right and wrong
– Multiplayer planning with coding agents in GitHub Next's Chopin
– Human-to-agent handoffs, formal verification and spec-driven development
– Why software quality is rising, not falling, with coding agents
– Which roles still matter: PMs, designers and engineers

Chapters:
00:00:00 - Introduction
00:02:14 - Inside GitHub Next and the Chopin project
00:05:57 - Why solo agents break team alignment
00:07:52 - Why coding agents struggle with design

00:18:27 - Planning with coding agents as collaborators
00:26:49 - Multiplayer planning with background agents
00:31:57 - Agent handoffs and spec-driven development
00:37:41 - Quality, craft and who decides what to build

items.title: Bringing conversational analytics to Gemini with Agentic Data Cloud connectors
items.summary:
Data Cloud connectors in Gemini for business, now in preview, give business users and analysts a direct way to query live enterprise data in natural language. Across most organizations, data questions multiply faster than analysts can answer them: Projects stall in ticket queues, leaders fall back on guesswork, and unmanaged spreadsheets spread across teams. Early generative AI tools promised conversational access to data, but they often struggled to generate accurate SQL across complex schemas or to respect governance rules. Data Cloud connectors let you query governed data directly from your workspace while enforcing row- and column-level security and respecting end-user credentials.

A new way to query enterprise data

Gemini brings conversational analytics directly into your day-to-day workflow through two paths: Conversational Analytics agents, which let you create data agents that include context and instructions to effectively answer questions for specific use cases, and Data Cloud connectors, allowing you to query live data directly with Gemini. End users can pull data directly from BigQuery (preview), operational databases like Spanner, AlloyDB, and Cloud SQL (preview), and governed data from Looker (preview). From there, you can move your findings directly into everyday tools, such as turning query results into a Google Doc, an email draft in Gmail, or a deck in Google Slides.

How Data Cloud connectors work

Data Cloud connectors work with Knowledge Catalog to locate relevant data, interpret your question, and execute permission-scoped queries under your identity.

When you ask a question in Gemini, the system coordinates discovery, semantic interpretation, and query execution, using the following capabilities:

  1. Natural-language question: You ask an exploratory question in plain language (for example, "How many sales did we have this month for all cold weather products?"). End users aren’t expected to know the table or project to use.

  2. Semantic discovery: Gemini searches Knowledge Catalog to locate candidate data across your estate, considering key attributes like usage patterns.

  3. Context mapping: The system uses technical metadata, business glossaries, and semantic models to map everyday terms into exact database structures, such as resolving "cold weather products" to specific categories like sweaters, coats, and jackets in an ecommerce catalog.

  4. Permission-aware execution: Gemini generates a SQL query and runs it through the connector under your user credentials, respecting your existing row- and column-level database permissions.

To accurately navigate an enterprise data estate, language models need business context alongside raw database access. Knowledge Catalog provides a curated context bundle, including technical metadata, business logic, table relationships, and verified queries, that improves query accuracy while reducing latency and token consumption.

Enterprise analytics has long been fragmented by physical borders: data locked in proprietary silos, open lakehouse tables in cloud object storage, and datasets distributed across multicloud environments. Beyond native BigQuery storage, the BigQuery connector brings conversational analytics to a borderless lakehouse, unifying these environments into a single conversational interface to query open table formats (including Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, and Parquet) and cross-cloud datasets in AWS or Azure using BigQuery. The connector inherits fine-grained access policies from BigQuery and Knowledge Catalog, so row- and column-level access controls apply whether you query native tables or open lakehouse files.

Choosing between connectors and data agents

In addition to using direct Data Cloud connectors to query data in plain language, you can also use Conversational Analytics agents to enable these experiences. While Data Cloud connectors allow you to provide exploratory and ad hoc analysis for users, conversational analytics agents are scoped agents that are built and certified directly by data teams within your organization. These can be built across Data Cloud products such as BigQuery, Looker, and operational databases including Spanner, AlloyDB, and Cloud SQL.

These pre-configured agents allow users to run highly governed, multi-step strategic analyses that are scoped to particular subsets of data, supporting compliance requirements and predictable results for reporting. These data agents can also be published in Gemini for consumption or made available via API for building your own conversational apps in the enterprise.

These approaches are complementary. Gemini direct connectivity also surfaces relevant published agents created by central data teams, so users can decide whether to proceed with ad hoc analysis using the connectors or use the scoped agent. You can choose the right approach for each workload.

Built-in access controls and governance

Data Cloud connector queries execute under the end user’s identity. An employee without access to executive salary data or protected healthcare records cannot query that data through natural-language prompts. The agent only discovers metadata in Knowledge Catalog to which you have access, and only executes queries that your account has permission to run.

How to create Data Cloud connectors

Administrators can configure Data Cloud connectors in the Gemini admin console. From there, admins set up default read-only connections to datasets in BigQuery, operational databases, or Looker, with Knowledge Catalog enabled automatically. Once configured, end users can enable the connector in Gemini to start querying data and building reports in plain language.

Setup documentation is available for the BigQuery, Spanner, Cloud SQL, and AlloyDB for PostgreSQL connectors, with Looker also in preview.

Unlike data ingestion mode, which copies data into a Gemini data store, Data Cloud connectors use federated query mode to query your data in place without copying or indexing it — using Knowledge Catalog automatically to search accessible metadata and look up business context.

Why use Data Cloud connectors over custom MCP

Compared to connecting to public or self-managed Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, first-party Data Cloud connectors provide two main advantages:

  1. Built-in skills for higher response quality: Data Cloud connectors include pre-configured agent skills tailored to each data engine, such as advanced SQL and AI function generation for BigQuery and operational databases, to improve query accuracy and response quality.

  2. Guided setup and managed authentication: First-party connectors provide a guided setup experience with managed authentication for Google Cloud databases and BigQuery, removing the need to deploy MCP middleware or manage your own OAuth client configuration for Google Cloud services. In addition, connector-specific settings, such as specifying a default Google Cloud billing project for BigQuery query execution, help administrators enforce governance and manage query costs.

Get started today

Data Cloud connectors help teams find answers from enterprise data sources without waiting on backlog queues. To get started, review the Data Cloud connectors documentation or explore Conversational Analytics agents.

items.title: claude-code v2.1.317
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added a warning to /schedule when a new cloud scheduled task gets connectors you did not ask for, with how to remove them
  • Added a check that asks before a web or shell tool call sends your account email address to the network
  • Added onFailure: "block" for Agent SDK hook callbacks, so a callback that fails blocks the action instead of letting it run
  • Added a notice in Claude Desktop's Code tab when your organization's remote managed settings haven't loaded for the session, and another once they do
  • Added a notice when auto mode's check has no answer for a subagent's tool call, which used to leave nothing in the main view
  • Added anthropic.plan, anthropic.seat_type, anthropic.provider and anthropic.custom_base_url to OTel metrics, events and spans
  • Added a cost report to the Claude apps gateway admin API, GET /v1/organizations/analytics/cost, for reading past spend over a date range in total, per developer, per day or per IdP group
  • Added a daily record of each developer's IdP groups on Claude apps gateways with admin: set, kept for admin.identity_retention_days, which the cost report groups by
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NESTED_SESSION_ID: set it to 1 on a self-hosted runner to have claude -p run inside a session use that session's ID and transcript, as in earlier versions
  • Fixed project and local MCP servers disconnecting after the first turn in some Claude desktop sessions
  • Fixed auto mode failing every turn when an LLM gateway set as the base URL answers 403 or 422 to its server-side safety check (a 403 with an apiKeyHelper is unchanged)
  • Fixed claude auth status exiting before a slow token refresh was saved, which could sign you out on the next run
  • Fixed a project's effortLevel setting being ignored by sessions that an app starts ahead of time and then opens in the project, such as new sessions in the desktop app's Code tab
  • Fixed claude --from-pr reporting "No conversations found" in projects with many sessions when the linked session was older than the first page
  • Fixed the second of two simultaneous permission prompts showing no file path or command on claude.ai and the mobile apps
  • Fixed Remote Control and SDK hosts offering "don't ask again" on a mod's tool calls
  • Fixed session titles being lost in cloud and SDK sessions when a new message or Stop arrived while the title was generating
  • Fixed self-paced /loop wakeups sometimes not being scheduled when Claude left a field out of its request
  • Fixed auto mode in cloud sessions stopping for approval when the Artifact tool uploaded, wrote to a database or saved a file through the outputs folder
  • Fixed skills synced from claude.ai being lost or downloaded again every ten minutes when they can't be written to disk
  • Fixed /schedule leaving a cloud scheduled task's next run time and link out of its results after creating or updating it
  • Fixed screen readers speaking a running subagent's elapsed time and token count on every change in screen reader mode
  • Fixed a region or network block (HTTP 403) being shown as a sign-in failure; the error now explains the block
  • Fixed Claude saying a working claude.ai connector needed authorization or had failed in cloud sessions when a synced plugin included the same server
  • Fixed claude -p exiting 0 when a full disk or quota lost its transcript or ~/.claude.json writes; it now prints an error and, in text and json output, exits 1. Full NFS exports may be missed
  • Fixed edits to settings files made in the first second or so after launch not taking effect until a settings file changed again
  • Fixed old transcripts not being cleaned up on machines where some runs skip cleanup, such as runs using --setting-sources
  • Fixed deleted agent team inboxes being re-created by a teammate's late message
  • Fixed a re-created agent teammate being removed from its team by an earlier shutdown approval
  • Fixed stored scheduled tasks being impossible to list or delete after scheduled tasks were turned off
  • Fixed Claude deleting your most recently updated /team-onboarding guide when asked to delete one without naming which
  • Fixed Claude saying a /team-onboarding guide was deleted when the server refused the delete
  • Fixed the Claude apps gateway hiding Amazon Bedrock's "Input is too long." error, which left sessions failing every turn with "upstream rejected the request" instead of compacting
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions losing recent turns or the whole conversation when restarted while a plan waited for approval
  • Fixed "Prompt is too long" after automatic compaction in sessions whose very large CLAUDE.md changed since it was last sent
  • Fixed high memory use and slow startup in headless sessions with many plugins that register commands
  • Fixed stdio MCP servers receiving an empty AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK when their env config sets it to empty; the variable is now unset, so the server can use the machine's own AWS credentials
  • Fixed API requests failing with "unable to get local issuer certificate" behind some TLS-inspecting proxies after a root certificate renewal
  • Fixed very long conversations losing their earlier summary when compaction had to shorten its own request
  • Fixed a PDF's own metadata being able to make Read and @-mentions under-count its pages
  • Fixed DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_OPUS and DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_SONNET having no effect on [1m], other-region and undated spellings of the default model
  • Fixed /artifacts and the Artifact tool's shared list showing no shared artifacts when you have 200 or more of your own
  • Fixed Claude treating partial Grep and Glob results as complete when a search hit its time limit
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry exports to an https:// endpoint through a proxy never being sent when they started while another export was still in progress
  • Fixed a flood of connection attempts to a proxy that blocks (HTTP 403) OpenTelemetry exports to an http:// endpoint
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry exports hanging indefinitely behind a proxy that never answers; they now time out after 10 seconds, or OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT up to 30 seconds
  • Fixed resumed sessions telling Claude again about a file change it already knew about
  • Fixed Claude sometimes not using a built-in tool in a resumed session after an earlier call failed because the tool was switched off
  • Fixed /remote-control answering "Unknown command" instead of saying that Remote Control is turned off by the disableRemoteControl setting
  • Fixed agent team teammates in tmux or iTerm2 panes starting in auto mode when the lead session was in manual mode
  • Fixed a background session sometimes losing a just-made change of permission mode when it was upgraded or retired
  • Fixed Ctrl+C stopping all running background agents when pressed to clear typed text at the prompt
  • Fixed /feedback showing "Enter to confirm" while a report is being sent
  • Fixed child processes of a stopped shell command sometimes being sent SIGTERM twice, which could make some programs skip their cleanup
  • Fixed claude -p run inside a cloud or self-hosted runner session sharing that session's ID: it wrote into the session's transcript, and a restart could resume the wrong conversation
  • Fixed claude -p run inside a cloud or self-hosted runner session generating a title of its own and sending it to that session
  • Improved the error shown on Microsoft Foundry when Azure credentials can't be loaded: it now says to check or refresh them, and reports as cloud_credential_error
  • Improved /design-sync to say up front when your design system has moved to Claude, and stop before building instead of failing at upload
  • Improved the startup error when a required Claude apps gateway can't be reached: it points to the network instead of a sign-in, and says when the gateway's TLS certificate can't be verified
  • Improved the "Resume this session with" hint shown at exit to repeat the flags you launched with (for example --chrome --debug) ahead of --resume
  • Improved how self-hosted runners recover from server errors: after a 5xx other than 501 or 529, a runner's next poll now opens a new connection instead of reusing the one that failed
  • Improved how self-hosted runner sessions recover from server errors: after a 5xx other than 501 or 529, a session now opens new connections instead of reusing the one that failed
  • Improved how self-hosted runner sessions recover when connections stop answering: after a heartbeat gets no answer, a session now opens new connections instead of trying each idle one in turn
  • Changed SendMessage so a message to a running background agent arrives earlier: its running command moves to the background, without being stopped
  • Changed subagents and teammates on a different model from the main conversation to use that model's saved effort level or its default, instead of the session's effort level
  • Changed exit to skip the "Background work is running" prompt for plugin monitors
  • Changed the built-in plugin-authoring skill to offer once, after a mod you built works, to help share the mod
  • Removed the Read tool's "file unchanged since your last Read" stub: reading an unchanged file again returns its content
  • Windows: Fixed every tool call being refused on some volumes where the native path lookup fails; the working-directory check now compares the folder's identity instead
  • Windows: Fixed the session scratchpad and other temporary paths growing with your project's path length in sessions not started by Claude Desktop, which made repositories cloned into them hit the 260-character path limit
  • Gateway: Fixed the status line and /usage showing a developer's own spend limit as 100% used after their group's pooled budget ran out
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed Claude not seeing the interrupted tool call when a session moves to a new runner and the turn is older than CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN_MAX_AGE_MS
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed an MCP server that was switched off coming back on after the session moved to a new machine, when the session service had refused to save the switch
  • Remote Control: Improved fork names when the app doesn't set one: a long name keeps its "(fork)" ending, and in sessions started with claude remote-control a fork of "Name (fork)" is "Name (fork 2)"
  • [VSCode] Fixed forked conversations dropping messages: only one of the tool calls Claude ran in parallel was kept, and the last messages a compaction kept were lost, which could leave Claude's answer without the question it answered
  • [VSCode] Fixed a message being lost when Claude did not finish starting in time: the extension now starts Claude once more before showing the error
  • [VSCode] Fixed the sign-in screen opening when a request is blocked for its region or network
  • [VSCode] Fixed the Account panel showing the plan name with a lower-cased second word
  • [VSCode] Fixed file links in a Claude tab opening on top of the chat instead of in another editor group
  • [VSCode] Fixed attachment chips, menus, banners and dialogs in the Claude panel staying small when chat.fontSize is raised
  • [VSCode] Fixed ultrathink not raising effort for its turn or showing its rainbow when telemetry is off
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a link card to cloud sessions, so you can open or decline a link an MCP server asks you to visit instead of the request going unseen
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed the organization environment dialog in admin settings to the personal dialogs' short layout: each section opens from a row, and unsaved input asks before closing
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed adding a network secret for a host that already has one silently replacing it; the Add secret form now refuses and points you to the existing secret
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed new scheduled tasks ignoring your organization's default environment: the form now starts on the one an admin chose instead of the Anthropic-hosted default
  • [Remote Control] Fixed the next message to an idle session going unanswered after you restart claude remote-control, when you sent it within a minute of your previous message
  • [Claude Tag] Changed newly pasted artifact links in Slack to show a simpler card with an Open button that opens the artifact in Claude, instead of Slack's side panel
release_highlights: Added a warning to /schedule when a new cloud scheduled task gets connectors you did not ask for, with how to remove them
Added a check that asks before a web or shell tool call sends your account email address to the network
Added onFailure: "block" for Agent SDK hook callbacks, so a callback that fails blocks the action instead of letting it run
